lesson.title: Länder II: die Schweiz, Österreich, die Türkei, Polen, Irland
lesson.subtitle: five more countries — two insist on their article, and the endings -ei, -land and -reich still mean what they meant

hook.title: The Row That Brings Its Own Article
hook.content: Länder I gave you five names that travel bare — nach Deutschland, aus Spanien. The second row splits in two: Österreich, Polen and Irland stay bare, while die Schweiz and die Türkei insist on carrying die. And the names themselves are little history lessons. die Schweiz is a country named after one canton: Schwyz was a member of the 1291 confederation, its people were so loud in the alliance's story that by the fifteenth century the whole union answered to their valley's name. Österreich is a compass reading: Ost + Reich, 'eastern realm' — the same Ost as your compass word der Osten, and the same reich you met inside Frankreich, the k→ch twin of English rich; the old royal names kept it too, as the -ric in Theodoric. die Türkei is built with the place-suffix -ei, the same one that turns backen into die Bäckerei: the place of the Turks. Polen keeps its Slavic story — the Polanie, 'the plain-dwellers', the people of the open field. And Irland is English Ireland with one letter gone: German heard the name and simply kept it, with the purest cognate pair in the language at the end, Land ↔ land.

footnotes.title: One Country, Four Languages
footnotes.content: die Schweiz has four national languages: German, French, Italian and Romansh. The next lesson hands you three of those four names — which is one reason Swiss schoolchildren would find your German homework very reasonable.

pattern.title: Countries in Frames, Articles Attached
pattern.content: The three frames from Länder I still do all the work — only the cases change. 1. Dwell: Ich wohne in der Schweiz, Ich wohne in Polen — dwelling takes in + dative, and the dative of die is der. 2. Move: Ich fahre nach Österreich, Ich fahre in die Türkei — bare names ride after nach, and movement keeps in + die, the accusative: in der is where you are, in die is where you are going. 3. Originate: Meine Familie kommt aus Polen, Irland ist grün und schön. Time drops into position 1 as always: Im März fahre ich nach Österreich, Im Januar bin ich in der Schweiz — im is in + dem, the month's own little contraction.
pattern.linguist_note: The place-suffixes are old money. -land is the Germanic land (England, Irland, Deutschland — one recipe, three countries), -ei is Latin -ia in German clothes (Türkei, Bäckerei), and -reich is the old ruler-word. English writes the same Latin suffix as -y: Turkey, Hungary, Italy — the ending is identical, only the costume changed.

exercises.prompt: The second row of countries — match each sentence with its reading:

matching_pairs.english: In January I am in Austria
matching_pairs.german: Im Januar bin ich in Österreich
Der Urlaub war in der Türkei

matching_pairs.english: In November Ireland is gray, in December I am in Switzerland
matching_pairs.german: Im November ist Irland grau, im Dezember bin ich in der Schweiz

matching_pairs.english: The hotel is in Switzerland, the ferry to Ireland
matching_pairs.german: Das Hotel ist in der Schweiz, die Fähre nach Irland

matching_pairs.english: Poland and Switzerland on the map
matching_pairs.german: Polen und die Schweiz auf der Karte

matching_pairs.english: The color of Ireland is green

exercises.target_answer: Ich wohne in der Schweiz, Im Januar bin ich in Österreich, Meine Familie kommt aus Polen, Der Urlaub war in der Türkei, Irland ist grün und schön, Im November ist Irland grau, im Dezember bin ich in der Schweiz, Das Hotel ist in der Schweiz, die Fähre nach Irland, Polen und die Schweiz auf der Karte, Irland ist fern, Die Farbe Irlands ist grün, Österreich ist im Osten, In Irland essen wir Fisch
exercises.meaning: live in, travel to, come from, vacation in, is beautiful
exercises.explanation: Three countries ride bare (Österreich, Polen, Irland), two bring their own die (Schweiz, Türkei) and turn in der. The frames are the ones from Länder I: in for dwelling, aus for coming, nach for going.

exercises.prompt: Which of these country names refuses to travel without its article?
exercises.meaning: die Türkei is one of the two feminines — die Schweiz is the other
exercises.explanation: die Türkei and die Schweiz are feminine and carry die everywhere: in der Türkei, in der Schweiz. Österreich, Polen and Irland are neuter and go bare, like all of Länder I.

exercises.prompt: 'Österreich' ends in 'Reich' ('realm/empire'), whose k→ch consonant shift mirrors 'Buch/book'. Which four-letter English adjective meaning 'wealthy' is the twin of 'reich'?
exercises.meaning: reich ↔ rich: one ruler-word, two outcomes
exercises.explanation: Both descend from the same Germanic ruler-word: German kept the ruler and the realm (das Reich) alongside the money sense, while English narrowed the word to wealth. reach is a different root that happens to rhyme, realm came from Latin through French — and right is unrelated.

exercises.prompt: Assemble: 'I am traveling to Austria in March'
exercises.target_answer: Im März fahre ich nach Österreich
exercises.meaning: I am traveling to Austria in March
exercises.explanation: The month phrase takes position 1 and pushes fahre to slot 2 — the swap from the time lessons. im is in + dem, and the bare Österreich rides after nach with no article to slow it down.

exercises.prompt: Assemble: 'I am traveling to Poland in February'
exercises.target_answer: Im Februar fahre ich nach Polen
exercises.meaning: I am traveling to Poland in February

vocab_hints.note: im is in + dem, fused into one word — months take it bare: im Januar, im März, im Februar. The feminine countries never fuse: in der Schweiz (dwelling), in die Türkei (going).

exercises.explanation: Same frame, one country over: Im Februar fahre ich nach Polen. The bank's leftovers prove the frame scales — the month swaps (Januar), the country swaps (Türkei), the frame never notices.

summary.outcome: Name five more countries, use them with in, nach and aus — articles attached for the two feminines — and read the -ei, -land and -reich endings as the old words they are.

use_example.german: Im März fahre ich nach Österreich — im Januar war ich in der Schweiz.
use_example.english: In March I am traveling to Austria — in January I was in Switzerland.

summary.takeaway: die Schweiz and die Türkei wear die; Österreich, Polen and Irland go bare. Österreich is 'eastern realm' with rich inside it, die Türkei is Türk + -ei like Bäckerei, and Irland kept Ireland's name.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Next: die Sprache and the four language names — and the ending -isch that turns out to be English's own -ish.

twist.prompt: Without looking back — rebuild the core sentence from Länder II: die Schweiz, Österreich, die Türkei, Polen, Irland (I am traveling to Poland in February):
twist.target_answer: Im Februar fahre ich nach Polen
twist.explanation: Re-assembling "Im Februar fahre ich nach Polen" from scratch locks in the structural pattern of Länder II: die Schweiz, Österreich, die Türkei, Polen, Irland without relying on short-term echo.

schweiz.etymology_derivation: die Schweiz is named after Schwyz, the canton the country takes its name from. [wiktionary]

österreich.etymology_derivation: Old element for "east" + rīhhi "realm" — the eastern realm (Reich ↔ rich). [wiktionary]

türkei.context_phrase: Der Urlaub war in der Türkei.
türkei.etymology_derivation: Land of the Turks: from Medieval Latin Turcia, influenced by Türke "Turk". [wiktionary]

polen.etymology_derivation: Middle High German Polen, plural of Pole — land of the Poles. [wiktionary]

irland.etymology_derivation: The same name as English Ireland — land of the Irish, shared proper name. [wiktionary]

früh.etymology_derivation: Proto-West Germanic *frō(ī); only Dutch/Low German cognates listed. [UNVERIFIED — check] [wiktionary]

januar.etymology_derivation: Latin loan both English and German borrowed (via French): Latin Iānuārius. [wiktionary]

februar.etymology_derivation: Latin loan both English and German borrowed (via French): Latin Februārius. [wiktionary]

märz.etymology_derivation: Latin loan both languages share: Latin Martius via Middle High German merze. [wiktionary]

feiertag.context_phrase: Heute ist ein Feiertag, alles ist zu.
feiertag.context_translation: Today is a public holiday, everything is closed.
feiertag.etymology_derivation: Feier + Tag — literally celebration day; Tag is the twin of day (d → t). [wiktionary]

datum.etymology_derivation: Borrowed from Latin datum, literally something given — the same Latin participle that gave English date, from the Roman letter formula given at Rome. [wiktionary] [etymonline]

november.etymology_derivation: Latin loan both languages share: Latin November, inherited via Middle High German. [wiktionary]

grau.etymology_derivation: Proto-West Germanic *grāu — English gray is the same Germanic word. [wiktionary]

dezember.etymology_derivation: Latin loan both languages share: Latin december, inherited via Middle High German. [wiktionary]

hotel.etymology_derivation: Borrowed from French hôtel — the same French loan as English hotel. [wiktionary]

fern.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *ferrai — the same word as English far (see der Fernseher, far-seer). [wiktionary]

karte.context_phrase: Ich brauche eine Karte für die U-Bahn.
karte.context_translation: I need a ticket for the underground.
karte.etymology_derivation: From Latin charta through Old French carte — the page compares English card: the same paper-word, borrowed in both languages. [wiktionary]

fähre.context_phrase: Die Fähre fährt über den Fluss.
fähre.context_translation: The ferry goes across the river.
fähre.etymology_derivation: From Proto-Germanic *farjo, the ferrying word of the same far-root as fahren — the page lists English ferry as cognate. [wiktionary]

mütze.etymology_derivation: From Medieval Latin almutia 'hood, cowl' — a Romance loan; no English cognate. [wiktionary]

lila.etymology_derivation: From French lilas — a French loan in German; English lilac comes from the same French/Arabic source. [wiktionary]

rosa.etymology_derivation: Latin rosa loaned by both languages — English pink via French rose, same Latin source. [wiktionary]

farbe.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *farwō 'color' (Old High German farawa), from the PIE root *perḱ- 'colored'; no English cognate is listed on the page. [wiktionary]

grün.context_phrase: Im Sommer ist das Gras grün.
grün.context_translation: In summer the grass is green.
grün.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *grōniz, the root of grow; English green is the same Germanic word. [wiktionary]

frankreich.etymology_derivation: Franke "Frank" + Reich "realm" — realm of the Franks. [wiktionary]

italien.etymology_derivation: The same Latin name Italia as English Italy; shared proper name, no sound shift to fake. [wiktionary]

spanien.etymology_derivation: The same Latin name Hispania that English Spain descends from, via Old High German Spānia. [wiktionary]

osten.context_phrase: Der Wind kommt aus dem Osten.
osten.context_translation: The wind comes from the east.
osten.etymology_derivation: From Old High German ostan, from Proto-Germanic *austrą — the same root as English east, ultimately from the dawn root *ausos, as in Latin aurora. [wiktionary]

fisch.context_translation: The fish swims in the water.

fahrkarte.context_phrase: Ich kaufe eine Fahrkarte nach Berlin.
fahrkarte.context_translation: I buy a ticket to Berlin.
fahrkarte.etymology_derivation: fahren (to travel, the fare root) + Karte (card, from Latin charta — the same loan as English card): a travel-card. [wiktionary]

abfahrt.context_phrase: Die Abfahrt ist um neun Uhr.
abfahrt.context_translation: The departure is at nine o'clock.
abfahrt.etymology_derivation: The noun of abfahren: ab (off) + Fahrt (the fare root) — literally an off-driving, a departure. [wiktionary]

ankunft.context_phrase: Die Ankunft ist um halb sieben.
ankunft.context_translation: The arrival is at half past six.
ankunft.etymology_derivation: From ankommen (to arrive) — an on-coming; kommen is the German twin of come. [wiktionary]

flughafen.etymology_derivation: Flug (flight) + Hafen (port) — the flight-port; see der Fernseher-style calques. [wiktionary]

ausflug.context_phrase: Wir machen einen Ausflug in die Berge.
ausflug.context_translation: We take a trip to the mountains.
ausflug.etymology_derivation: aus (out) + Flug (flight, from fliegen — English fly): literally an out-flight, an excursion. [wiktionary]

tourist.context_phrase: Der Tourist fragt nach dem Weg.
tourist.context_translation: The tourist asks for the way.
tourist.etymology_derivation: Tour (tour, turn) + -ist; the page says it was formed in the 18th century, possibly influenced by English tourist being made at the same time from the same French material. [wiktionary]

england.etymology_derivation: From Old English Engla land — land of the Angles. [wiktionary]

deutschland.etymology_derivation: diutsch "of the people" + lant "land" — compound: land of the people. [wiktionary]

urlaub.context_phrase: Ich fahre im Urlaub nach Italien.
urlaub.context_translation: I go to Italy on vacation.
urlaub.etymology_derivation: Middle High German urloup 'permission to be away', kin to erlauben — cognate with English leave. [wiktionary]

fahren.context_translation: I am going / driving to Berlin.
fahren.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *faraną — the twin of English fare (farewell, bus fare, 'how did you fare?'). [wiktionary]

familie.etymology_derivation: Borrowed from Latin familia — the same Latin source as English family. [wiktionary]

sache.context_translation: That is my affair / thing (for my sake).

reichen.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *raikijaną — English reach is the documented cognate; the old k softened to ch (the velar shift). [wiktionary]

th_to_d.name: The Dental Shift (TH → D)
th_to_d.historical_linguistics: Every single original Germanic "th" sound systematically shifted to "d" in High German, while English kept the ancient "th".
th_to_d.philological_note: Around 500–700 AD in the High German Consonant Shift, dental fricatives hardened into voiced dental stops.

d_to_t.name: The Stop Shift (D → T)
d_to_t.historical_linguistics: Where English kept Germanic "d", High German hardened it into "t".
d_to_t.philological_note: Voiced stops became voiceless. Explains pairs like day ↔ Tag, door ↔ Tür, and drink ↔ trinken.
d_to_t.literature_source: Complementary to the TH → D shift: as TH took over D, original D shifted to T in High German.

p_to_pf_f.name: The Labial Shift (P → PF / F)
p_to_pf_f.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /p/ shifted to the affricate "pf" at the beginning of words, and to "f" or "ff" after vowels.
p_to_pf_f.philological_note: Explains apple ↔ Apfel, pepper ↔ Pfeffer, hope ↔ hoffen, and sleep ↔ schlafen.

t_to_s_ss_z.name: The Sibilant Shift (T → S / SS / Z)
t_to_s_ss_z.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /t/ shifted to sibilant "s/ss/ß" after vowels, and to "z" (/ts/) at the beginning of words.
t_to_s_ss_z.philological_note: Reveals water ↔ Wasser, eat ↔ essen, better ↔ besser, two ↔ zwei, and to ↔ zu.
t_to_s_ss_z.literature_source: Walter Skeat - Primary dental affrication and spirantization

k_to_ch.name: The Velar Shift (K → CH)
k_to_ch.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /k/ softened to the fricative "ch" in medial and final positions.
k_to_ch.philological_note: The Ach-Laut [x] occurs after a, o, u; the Ich-Laut [ç] occurs after e, i, ä, ö, ü.

v_to_b.name: The Bilabial Shift (V / F → B)
v_to_b.historical_linguistics: Intervocalic /v/ and /f/ in English regularly correspond to voiced /b/ in German.
v_to_b.philological_note: Explains give ↔ geben, live ↔ leben, love ↔ lieben, over ↔ über, and seven ↔ sieben.
v_to_b.literature_source: Proto-Germanic bilabial spirant closing to stop in High German

y_gh_to_g_ch.name: The Palatal & Guttural Link (Y → G & GH → CH)
y_gh_to_g_ch.historical_linguistics: English vocalized palatal "g" into "y" (say, day, yesterday) and silenced "gh" (night, laugh, light). German preserved them as "g" or "ch".
y_gh_to_g_ch.philological_note: Explains why English spelling has silent 'gh' letters — they were original German-like gutturals!

latin_ieren.name: The Latin / Romance Layer (-ate / -ize → -ieren)
latin_ieren.phonetic_rule: English verbs ending in -ate, -ize, -ify, -ish ➔ German verbs ending in -ieren
latin_ieren.historical_linguistics: English verbs derived from Latin or French directly map to German verbs ending in -ieren.
latin_ieren.philological_note: Past participles of -ieren verbs never take the "ge-" prefix (studieren → studiert).
latin_ieren.literature_source: Middle High German productive loan suffix from Old French -ier

strong_verbs_ablaut.name: The 7 Strong Verb Classes (Ablaut)
strong_verbs_ablaut.phonetic_rule: English irregular strong verbs with internal vowel changes ➔ German strong verbs following the exact same Ablautreihe
strong_verbs_ablaut.historical_linguistics: Shared 7 Proto-Germanic verb classes where tenses are formed by shifting root vowels.
